design_rule.statement: Every apparent miracle in this franchise has visible hardware. Wherever an image looks magical, the mount, cable, battery, lens, hinge, seam or fixing that produces it must be findable in the same image.
design_rule.why: Design document §2.1 forbids real supernatural effect, and OPERATIONS.md §4 makes that the franchise differentiator. Turning it into a DRAWING rule (not just a story rule) also defeats the three named wardrobe failures in references/wardrobe-questions.md — hardware has construction, and a featureless bodysuit does not.
design_rule.applies_to: every character, every asset, including CGs and hero shots

style_bible.medium_anchor: Anime illustration, clean linework and cel colour. — ONE clause, used verbatim. Do not expand it.
style_bible.render: Otherwise let the generator work in its own default idiom. Do NOT specify tone counts, gradient behaviour, rim light, or flatness targets.
style_bible.value_range: Full range, both ends named SEPARATELY. Darks to true black; highlights blown to near-white on a NAMED lit object (a toe cap, a cheekbone, tape in the hair, a metal edge). Adjectives alone produce weak highlights — measured: 'very bright' gave p98=177, naming the lit objects gave p98=246.
style_bible.contrast_note: This is VALUE contrast, distinct from the saturation work. Both apply.
style_bible.correction_note: REWRITTEN 2026-07-27 (owner: 'what it outputs without stylization is better... work with nanobanana default style constraints'). Two failure poles were measured: zero style language defaults to PHOTOREALISM, and long style blocks produced the 2.5D look. One short medium anchor sits between them and preserves the generator's own strengths.

Corrected 2026-07-27 — the previous 'landscape-coloured' answer was the dullest palette in the cast (mean saturation 0.25) and was wrong twice over: it contradicted design-canon.md §3 ('bright, saturated palettes read well at scale'), and it was bad in-world reasoning. People who live in milk fog and steep terrain do NOT dress to blend into it — mountain rescue, hill walkers and village festival dress are all deliberately high-visibility, because being findable is survival. The mountain community wears the colour of the water it is fighting for (bright spring turquoise/jade) plus saffron and lacquer red so it can be seen at fifty metres in cloud. Brighter than any other faction, and the most rational palette in the cast.

ensemble_note: The cast was coloured together, not sequentially (design-canon §3), then MEASURED rather than eyeballed. Area-weighted greyscale luma over the 11 zones gives: LIGHT — splash .72, momo .70, kurogane .52, stella .51, saya .45; MID — aster7 .38, kitsune .35, miya .31, ryuki .26, hana .26, yuki .23, ren .21, lumina .19; DARK — reika .13. Honest caveat: this is a MID-heavy roster, not the even three-way split it would be convenient to claim. Only Reika is genuinely dark-dominant. That is acceptable because value is the second differentiator here, not the first — all 91 character pairs differ in at least two of {silhouette class, dominant hue, shape majority, head-ratio band}, and all 14 silhouette classes are unique.

greyscale_collisions.method: area-weighted luma per design-canon §3 area-effect note; pairs closer than 0.03 would merge in a greyscale roster check
greyscale_collisions.note: These six pairs are NOT design faults — each is separated by silhouette class and by hue. They are STAGING constraints: when two of a pair share a frame, the shot must lean on silhouette and hue separation, or push one figure's lighting, because value alone will not part them.

What do they wear when it rains? When it is cold? Seirin is a coastal city with real weather.

answers.wardrobe: An adult's oil-slate coverall, inherited from the workshop's dead-stock rail and cut down by her own hand to jacket length — the cut edge is raw and fraying, not hemmed. She wears it off both shoulders with the empty sleeves knotted across her waist, over a bleached undershirt, forearms wrapped in cloth strapping against hot metal. The clothes came from the workshop, not from a shop; nothing was bought new. In rain she borrows a port oilskin several sizes too big. In cold a quilted hanten goes UNDER the coverall so the decals stay showing. Second outfit: an oversized secondhand track jacket, which is what she wears when she is not allowed to work — she looks younger in it and resents that. Everything is stained at the cuff and knee; the knees are the newest fabric because they are patched most often. The coverall was chosen by her only in the sense that she chose to cut it: it was never her size and never will be, and that is the point — she is wearing an adult's job.
answers.wardrobe_sources: Mechanic coveralls and Japanese noragi/sashiko work-repair tradition, plus port fishing oilskins. Plausible because she works in a Tetsuba repair shop where dead-stock workwear is the cheapest clothing available to her; her family lost house and work after the plant accident, so bought clothing is not on the table. Construction: heavy cotton-poly twill, front zip plus three press studs, patch pockets bar-tacked at the corners, sleeves set with a felled seam — so when she knots them at the waist the seam ridge shows and the knot holds its shape rather than draping like jersey. The hanten is layered under, not over, and is quilted, so it changes her silhouette by thickening the torso rather than adding an outline. Not a bodysuit and not sci-fi armour: she wears the actual garment her actual trade issues.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.1 dock accident — coverall, oil-wet, no lanyard (she is not cleared, and the audience should notice). Sc.4 rain — the borrowed oilskin over the coverall, hood down because it blocks her hearing. Sc.6 strike — coverall with the lanyard, first time; she keeps touching it. Sc.9 hearing — the track jacket, because an adult told her to look like a child, and she is furious. Sc.12 festival — coverall with hanten under, lanyard on, decals wet with rain. She never fully changes on screen; the visible changes are the lanyard appearing and the oilskin going on and off. The oilskin gets torn at the dock and stays torn. On screen with Reika she must not merge: Reika is cold gunmetal and vertical, Ren is warm oxide and top-heavy.
answers.function_and_climate: Yes — the off-shoulder knot exists so she can free her arms in a second, and the cut-down length keeps the hem out of machinery, which is the actual reason such coats get shortened. Coastal Honshū: oilskin in rain, hanten under the coverall in winter, sleeves knotted and undershirt only in humid summer. The forearm wraps are climate-and-trade, not taste: they absorb sweat and stop hot swarf. The boots are steel-toe because the workshop requires it, and they are the only item she did not modify.
answers.colour_zones: Main colour is oxide red #B5432A, stated as a decision: it is the colour of rust after it has been sanded and primed — damage that has been dealt with. It is NOT the largest area; oil slate #3A4A52 is. Head is exactly 3 colours (#C4501F hair, #EBC49A skin, #5C8A6B eyes). Body runs 8: slate, bleached cream, leather brown, sock grey, boot near-black, oxide decals, aluminium trim, and the conditional hi-vis. Reserved: hi-vis yellow #E4D33A on the supervision lanyard only — its presence means a licensed adult has cleared her. At full sprite size the slate reads darker than the swatch because it covers so much, so the decals are placed on the chest and upper arm where the light hits, keeping the oxide reading at its intended brightness.
answers.ensemble_colour: Iron Requiem's shared logic is oxide/oil-slate/hi-vis and visible repair. Ren deviates by being the WARM and patched member of it. Her nearest colour neighbour is Reika, same faction: the deliberate difference is temperature and value — Reika is cold gunmetal, dark, and vertically lean; Ren is warm, mid-value and top-heavy. In greyscale Reika sits a full band darker. Her second-nearest is Momo (both carry an orange-family accent); they separate on value, since Momo is light-dominant white and Ren is dark-dominant slate.

Her body shows the job: real forearm, grip and shoulder development, short nails, scarred knuckles, a solvent burn through one eyebrow. She is strong in the specific way that lifting awkward objects makes a person strong, not gym-shaped.

answers.wardrobe: Her father's indigo stage coat, which is a real illusionist's working garment: thermochromic dye, hidden pockets, hook-and-eye fastening down a concealed placket. It is years too big — shoulders past hers, cuffs turned back twice, hem at the ankle. Under it a cream shirt and heavy pleated trousers cut down by the same hurried adult who cut her hair. The clothes came from her father; nothing was chosen by her and nothing fits. Her second outfit is her school uniform, which fits perfectly and is the only time she is invisible, which she prefers. In rain a clear vinyl poncho over the top. In winter she finally does the coat up, plus a scarf a Tsukimachi neighbour knitted for her without asking. Worn out: the cuff edges, the elbow, and the dye itself, which has been touched so often on the shoulders that the pale handprints no longer fade back.
answers.wardrobe_sources: Stage-magic costume tradition — a performer's coat is engineered for concealment, so it has real construction to look at: hidden inner pockets, a placket over the fastening so no button interrupts the line, weighted hem so it hangs and swings on a turn. She owns it because her father wore it and is gone from her daily life. Cloth: mid-weight wool-blend faille, heavy enough to hang away from her body instead of clinging — which is what makes the bell silhouette and the light-gap under the shoulders work. Fastening is hook-and-eye, deliberately fiddly, so a 13-year-old doing it up is a small visible act of effort. Not a bodysuit; the opposite of one.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.1 — school uniform, in a crowd, unnoticed. Sc.4 rain — poncho over the coat, coat blooming cyan everywhere from humidity, and she keeps her arms crossed to hide it. Sc.5 testimony with an adult and a lawyer present — coat, belt done properly, fan in the pocket; she is dressed as her father for courage. Sc.9 hearing — school uniform again, chosen for her by adults. Sc.12 festival — coat, open, warm-blotched at both shoulders because two people hugged her that evening, and that is the whole emotional payload of the shot. The coat is never removed on screen after Sc.5. She shares frames with Lumina, who is also indigo-and-gold: Hana is small, matte, and blotched; Lumina is tall, pressed, and lit.
answers.function_and_climate: The story asks her to observe, write, wait and eventually speak — never to run or fight, and the coat is deliberately impractical for anything athletic, which is honest. Coastal Honshū: vinyl poncho in rain, coat buttoned plus scarf in winter, coat carried over the arm in humid summer because she will not leave it behind. The thermochromic dye is a climate detail as much as a story one — it blooms in humidity and in a warm room, so the coat is a visible thermometer of the space she is in.
answers.colour_zones: Main colour indigo #2B2F6B, decided: the colour of a stage before the lights come up — potential, not spectacle. Head is exactly 3 (#2E3350 hair, #F0D9C4 skin, and the eyes, which are the earned exception: #D9A441 amber and #6C8AA6 grey-blue count as one zone carrying two values, and the extra complexity is justified because heterochromia is canon and is her secondary hook). Body runs 7. Reserved: heat-bloom cyan #6FE3E8, which appears only where warmth has touched the cloth. At full size the indigo reads darker than the swatch (area effect), which is why the cream shirt and the pale bloom are essential — without them she becomes a silhouette with a face.
answers.ensemble_colour: The Chorus of the Abyss reads indigo-plus-warm-gold, where the gold is always a lamp somebody is holding. Hana wears the faction's indigo but has no gold at all — she is inside the group's colour and outside its light, which is the entire point of her arc. Nearest cast member: Lumina, deliberately, because they must be readable as the same faction. The differences are value distribution and finish — Lumina is tailored, pressed and carries her own light source; Hana is oversized, matte and unlit. In greyscale Lumina has a hard bright point at chest height and Hana has none.
answers.physical_plausibility: 150 cm / 40 kg → BMI 17.8, which is around the median for a 13-year-old and is healthy — checked deliberately, because the failure case named in the wardrobe guide is exactly this age band. She is slight and still growing. Her posture is the real tell: shoulders drawn in, arms often crossed, weight on one hip — a child making herself smaller, not a stylised pose.

answers.wardrobe: White keikogi and slate hakama, because she teaches most mornings and does not change to run errands afterwards; over it a cedar-green field haori cut short enough to walk hill paths in. The hakama and keikogi are issued by the dōjō and mended by her. The haori is her own, bought in town, and is the only garment she picked for looks. She owns three outfits: the training one she lives in, a plain charcoal jacket-and-trousers for hearings, and a heavy winter layering. In rain, a mid-calf rain haori. Her hands are taped even out of the dōjō. Worn out: the hakama's rear pleat edges, the haori's shoulder where the tube strap sits, and the tube's own lacquer, which is chipped at the cap from being opened. All of it fits, all of it was chosen by her, and that steadiness is the character.
answers.wardrobe_sources: Japanese budō dress (keikogi, hakama, tabi) and rural noragi/hanten layering, with the haori shortened to a field length. Plausible for exactly this person in exactly this place: a 19-year-old instructor in a mountain community wears her work clothes all day because they ARE her clothes. Construction: the hakama is a pleated wrap with four ties, front and back, knotted at the waist — that visible knotting is the detail that keeps her from reading as generic; the keikogi is a wrap front with a cloth tie; the haori closes with a single braided cord, not buttons. Cloth is heavy cotton, stiff enough to hold the pleats as a shape rather than drape.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.1 — keikogi, hakama, tube, from the dōjō. Sc.4 rain — rain haori over everything, hakama hem dark with water and staying dark. Sc.7 blockade — same, tube prominent, hands taped, standing still. Sc.9 hearing — charcoal jacket and trousers, tube STILL on her back, which reads as a small refusal to be dressed by the occasion. Sc.12 festival — haori, hanten under, tube uncapped for the first time on screen, red end-cap showing. No change happens on screen and none is needed. Beside Ryuki, her student, they share the mountain green: Yuki is tall, vertical and matte; Ryuki is compact and carries a lacquered red-and-gold object.

answers.wardrobe: On an ordinary working day: an indigo noragi coat over an apron, sleeves corded back, hair up under a scarf — she runs a teahouse and that is what running a teahouse looks like. The festival rig comes out for events, streams and any night she needs the district to see her: vermilion overdress, cream blouse, gold sash, eared headdress, nine-tail yoke, paw boots. The rig is inherited — a touring-theatre costume the teahouse acquired generations back and never returned — and she has modified it herself, which is why the tail yoke's buckles and battery are visible and slightly inelegant. It fits her because she took it in; the shoulder seams show the alteration. Rain: a waxed haori over the top and clear covers over the tails. Winter: a padded hanten. answers.wardrobe_sources: Two traditions layered deliberately, which is why she looks unlike anything else in the cast. The rig is early-Shōwa touring-theatre costume with a Russian sarafan cut — a real historical crossover from Japan-Russia touring circuits, and a plausible thing for an old district's teahouse to own. Her working clothes are pure Japanese noragi and apron. Construction on the rig: a bib-fronted pinafore over a full-sleeved blouse, fastened with hooks at the left shoulder and a wide gold sash tied at the back over the yoke; the skirt is gored, so it bells without a hoop and swings on a turn. The tail yoke is a padded hip harness with nine sprung booms, cable-routed along each boom to a ring light, powered from a battery at the small of the back — that is real, buildable equipment, and it is drawn as such. Nothing here is a bodysuit and nothing is generic sci-fi.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.1 teahouse — noragi and apron. Sc.3 first 'miracle' — full rig, streaming, ring lights cyan, and she is the reason the audience gets clean footage of a staged event. Sc.4 rain — haori over the rig, tails bagged. Sc.5 safehouse — noragi again, and the change matters: she puts the rig away when people need to feel unobserved. Sc.9 hearing — noragi and a plain jacket, deliberately unremarkable. Sc.12 festival — full rig, everything lit, the district's own image of itself. The change from rig to noragi happens twice on screen and each time it means the same thing: cameras on, cameras off. In a group she is the widest silhouette in the cast, so blocking must give her horizontal room or she overlaps everyone.
answers.function_and_climate: The rig permits everything the story asks — walking, climbing teahouse stairs, carrying a tray, filming from nine angles — but it is heavy, and she should occasionally be seen adjusting the hip yoke or resting the weight, because equipment that never inconveniences anyone reads as magic. The paw boots are genuinely warm and genuinely bad in wet weather, and she complains about them.

answers.wardrobe: A quilted jade mountain jacket over a cream long-sleeve, dark trousers, hill boots and cotton gloves, all year. The jacket is village-made and has been passed down and re-quilted; the gloves are new and bought in packs, because she gets through them. She wears long sleeves and gloves for two honest reasons at once — the mountain is cold and wet, and her skin is more comfortable covered and moisturised — and the story should never resolve which reason is doing the work, because for her they are the same. Second outfit: the dragon-dance costume, a long articulated cloth body that needs a second operator, so her 'other outfit' cannot be worn alone. Rain: an oiled cape that covers her and the dragon head, and she keeps the head drier than herself. Winter: fleece hood and a second pair of gloves. answers.wardrobe_sources: Japanese mountain-village workwear — quilted noragi and hanten construction — plus the dragon-dance (ryū-mai) ceremonial tradition for the head and body costume. She owns them because she lives in the village that owns them; the head belongs to the community and is loaned to whoever dances. Construction: the jacket is hand-quilted in a grid, closes with cloth ties rather than buttons because ties are repairable, and the cuffs are ribbed to keep water out. The dragon head is lacquered papier-mâché over a bamboo frame with a hinged jaw and a cloth skirt at the neck — light enough for a sixteen-year-old to hold one-handed, which is why she can carry it everywhere, which is why it can be the memory point. Not a bodysuit, not sci-fi armour; every element is a real object with a real weight.

answers.wardrobe_sources: Not a garment tradition — laboratory and industrial-safety equipment: hi-vis mesh, asset tags, calibration glassware. Her surface is a colloidal gel with visible internal structure — micropump nodes, sensor beads, a faint manifold at the waist — so where another design would put fabric construction, she has mechanical construction, and there is genuinely something to look at up close. answers.costume_plot: Sc.1 dock — bare, no collar, because she is deployed before anyone files the paperwork, and Saya notices. Sc.3 lab — collar and tag on, in the safety enclosure. answers.function_and_climate: Her body permits exactly what the design document says CSR permits: entering narrow gaps, absorbing an impact, sorbing some contaminants, tactile inspection. It fails at exactly what the document says it fails at: heat, freezing, aggressive reagents, electromagnetic interference. Climate is not decoration for her, it is threat — coastal winter is genuinely dangerous, and the art shows it as stiffened surface, stilled tendrils and shortened streams rather than as dialogue. In humid summer she is at her best and her tendrils move most. Rain softens her outline. She is the only cast member whose weather response is a change of material rather than a change of clothes.

answers.wardrobe_sources: Not garment tradition — stage and event technology: drone light shows, volumetric projection onto haze, gobo and plane projection. That is the honest source and it is deliberately visible, because the franchise rule is that every miracle shows its hardware. The 'construction' to look at up close is the aircraft themselves: rotor guards, status LEDs, the charging contacts, the tripod projectors and their cable runs taped down across the ground. Anyone who looks past the pretty figure can see the entire mechanism, and the story rewards them for it.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.3 first 'omen' — full avatar over the harbour, at the perfect angle, and the city believes it. Sc.4 rain — most beautiful, least reliable, volume everywhere. Sc.7 staged omen — the avatar again, this time deliberately used to deceive, identical rendering, which is the uncomfortable point. Sc.8 someone walks around behind the projectors — off-axis shear, planes and aircraft, illusion over. Sc.10 charging rack — forty-one asleep. Sc.12 final image — the avatar on a wet wall after rain, resolving a watershed map into a constellation, rendered in white, because for once the data has been verified. That white is the ending.
answers.function_and_climate: She can do what a drone swarm and a projector can do: form patterns in air with a suitable medium, throw an image onto smoke, haze, rain or a wall, and visualise data at civic scale. She cannot do it in wind, cannot fly long without recharging, and cannot project onto nothing. Coastal Honshū weather is her whole physics: rain gives her volume and costs her stability, winter shortens her flight time so she visibly shrinks through an evening, and clear dry air makes her nearly invisible — she needs the city to be damp to be seen, which is a lovely and completely rational constraint.
answers.colour_zones: Main colour aurora violet #9A7FE0, decided — and pointedly, it was decided by a marketing department, not by her. The zone model applies only loosely and is mapped to light rather than cloth, with n/a stated honestly wherever there is nothing. Effective colour count is low: violet, cool white-blue, mint interference, plus the graphite of the unlit drone. Reserved: pure white #FFFFFF, used only for verified data — the most meaningful reserved colour in the cast. Area effect is inverted for her: she is emissive, so on a dark background she reads far brighter and larger than her swatch suggests, and on a light background she nearly disappears. Every Stella shot must therefore be composed against a dark or wet value, and that is a staging rule, not a preference.

answers.physical_plausibility: Height, weight and BMI are left null rather than invented, because she has no body — inventing them would be exactly the kind of fabricated stat this project's own guidance warns against. The numbers that DO matter and are fixed: forty-one aircraft, one permanently unlit; roughly eighteen minutes of flight per charge, which is why she shrinks through a long evening; two ground projectors. answers.wardrobe_sources: Aircrew and industrial fall-arrest harness design, plus flight-jacket and rescue-worker layering. Plausible because she IS ex-aircrew and this is the equipment she was trained in; keeping it is both practical and a refusal. Construction: the harness is real load-bearing webbing with steel triglide buckles, a chest strap, leg loops and a dorsal D-ring, and it must sit ON TOP of the jacket, with visible daylight under the straps — that is what stops it reading as decorative strapping, which is the single most common way this kind of design fails. The jacket has a two-way zip, knit cuffs and a bi-swing back for shoulder movement. Nothing smooth, nothing seamless, no glowing lines.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.1 dock — full kit, harness on, orange line coiled at the hip. Sc.4 telemetry raid — same, shell over the top, hood down in the rain. Sc.6 strike — harness over the bomber, standing between workers and private security, not touching anyone. Sc.9 hearing — she does not attend; the empty chair is the costume note. Sc.11 the flight suit on its hanger, in a locker, un-cut. Sc.12 festival — full kit, orange line deployed and actually used to pull someone clear, which is the payoff of the reserved colour. She is never out of the harness on screen. Beside Ren, same faction: Reika is cold, dark, vertical; Ren is warm, mid-value, top-heavy.
answers.function_and_climate: Yes, entirely — the harness is functional rescue equipment and the story asks her to climb, secure loads and pull people out, which she does with it. Coastal Honshū: technical shell in rain with the hood down, lined bomber in winter, base layer and harness alone in humid summer. The refusal to raise a hood is characterisation delivered through climate: she will be wet before she will be deaf and half-blind.

answers.wardrobe: A charcoal-indigo tailored suit, an ivory shell, flat polished shoes — the wardrobe of a senior crisis-communications consultant, which is what she was and, in every way that matters, still is. It fits perfectly, which is worth stating because almost nobody else's clothing in this cast fits: Ren's is too big, Hana's is too big, Miya's is askew, Splash's isn't hers. Lumina is the only person on screen wearing exactly what she chose, in her size, and that reads as control before a word is spoken. Second outfit: a plain indigo cardigan and skirt for shelter work, no lamp — and she is just as persuasive in it, which is the more disturbing fact. Rain: a navy trench, with someone else holding the umbrella because both her hands are on the lamp. Winter: a long charcoal coat, worn open. Nothing is worn out. Nothing is repaired. That is the tell.
answers.wardrobe_sources: Contemporary tailoring — corporate and political communications dress. Deliberately and explicitly NOT clerical: no robe, no cassock, no vestment, no sash. The wardrobe guide names priest-robe sci-fi as the single most common AI default, and this character is where a project like this would fall into it hardest, so the refusal is written into the banned list rather than left to judgement. Construction: half-canvassed jacket with a real roped shoulder, working cuff buttons, a single vent, and a lining in a colour only she ever sees — the last detail is the character in one seam. The ring light is a real object with a real switch, a real battery grip and a real charging port, because the visible-hardware rule applies most strictly to the person selling miracles.
answers.costume_plot: Sc.2 first 'cleansing' — suit, lamp, and the lamp is what makes the miracle; a viewer who watches the light rather than the woman can solve the scene. Sc.5 shelter — cardigan and skirt, no lamp, genuinely helping people, and this scene must not be undercut. Sc.7 staged omen — suit, lamp, coordinating with Akatomi. Sc.9 hearing — suit, lamp switched OFF and held anyway, which is the first time she is lit by someone else's light and the first time she looks 35. Sc.12 festival — suit, lamp on, and it fails; the battery dies at the wrong moment, and the crowd sees an ordinary woman holding a dead lamp. The lamp going out is her defeat, and it required no violence.
answers.function_and_climate: The suit permits everything the story asks: standing, speaking, walking a crowd, being photographed from any angle. She does nothing physical, ever, and the wardrobe says so honestly. Coastal Honshū: navy trench in rain, long wool coat in winter, jacket off and shell only in humid summer — and even in shirtsleeves she keeps both hands on the lamp. The flat shoes are a climate-and-function answer disguised as a character note: she walks a lot of wet pavement and she needs to be able to step down off a kerb without looking at her feet.
answers.colour_zones: Main colour warm gold #D8A94A — and the decision is that she MEANS a colour she does not wear. Her garments are all charcoal-indigo and ivory; the gold is emitted by an object she carries and can switch off. Head is exactly 3 (#6E5A46, #F0D6BE, #A88A5C). Body runs 6, which is low for an SSR and is correct: her density comes from tailoring detail and lighting, not from colour count. Reserved: the gold itself. Area effect: the dark suit at full size reads nearly black, which is exactly why the lamp is so effective — a small warm high-value source against a large dark mass, which is the most attention-grabbing arrangement available in the whole palette system, and she knows it.

They separate on value distribution, warmth and silhouette class: Momo has a warm amber accent and an A-line, Kurogane has a cold blue accent and a closed rectangle. In greyscale he is the flattest, most featureless light mass in the cast, which is exactly right.
answers.physical_plausibility: 178 cm / 78 kg → BMI 24.6, at the upper end of healthy — a big man who was physically active and now is not, which is both realistic for 48 and necessary for the silhouette. His life shows: an engineer's hands with old scars that no longer match his job, reading glasses he takes on and off, a heaviness through the shoulders, and shirts that fit a smaller man. He moves slowly and deliberately, and he is never drawn hunched or scheming — his posture is upright and reasonable, because he believes he is.

primary_question_set.note: Answered FIRST for every character. Derived from 27 primary sources with a principle-to-source attribution index, covering silhouette, kawaii/moe engineering, SD-chibi, physiognomic coding, transmedia flatness, worldview symbiosis, tiering, live-ops cadence, fan-art virality, merch and IP.
primary_question_set.supplement_rationale: It treats costume as a VARIABLE — how many variants per tier, what material — but never asks what the person actually wears on an ordinary day, where the clothes came from, or what they do in the rain. The `answers` block in each character record closes that gap.

silhouette_test.method: key out the #00B140 field, fill the figure 100% black, view at 64px (.venv-art, Pillow+numpy)
silhouette_test.headline: 3 outstanding, 4 strong, 2 good, 1 adequate, 4 needing amplification. No two silhouettes collide with EACH OTHER — the weakness is against a generic figure. The four weak ones (ren, momo, reika, lumina) all have memory points that are internal detail or small held objects, which a black fill deletes; the fix is to make each break the outer contour.

palette_policy.rule: BRIGHT AND SATURATED. Target mean zone saturation 0.50-0.65 with high value. Source: design-canon.md §3 area effect — a large area of a high-value colour reads MORE vivid than its swatch, so palettes chosen at swatch size come out dull at sprite size. Questionnaire A.2.3 additionally puts the kawaii band at HSL saturation 0.30-0.55 with lightness 0.70-0.90.
palette_policy.corrected: 2026-07-27. The first pass measured mean saturation 0.32 with 8/14 characters below 0.35 — dull. Every zone colour was re-specified brighter; mountain faction was rebuilt from scratch.
palette_policy.check: python3 - <<'EOF' … convert each zone hex to HSV and report the mean; anything under 0.40 is a defect.

generation_background.rule: Generate identity art on a BEAUTIFUL COLOURFUL BACKGROUND IN THE CHARACTER'S OWN PALETTE FAMILY — a soft gradient, an aurora wash, or a full atmospheric environment. Never a flat chroma-green field.
generation_background.why: Corrected 2026-07-27 on project-owner direction. The background is part of the generated image and CONDITIONS the model: a flat #00B140 field that appears in nobody's palette pushes the whole render toward desaturated, negative-space-poor colour, because the model harmonises the figure against the field it is given. The old rationale (green cannot contaminate the palette) optimised for a contamination risk that barely exists while paying a large, measurable cost in colour quality. A harmonious colourful ground makes the generator produce richer, better-lit, more saturated characters.
generation_background.how: Use a ground that AGREES with the character: aurora/gradient in their main colour and its neighbours, or a real environment from their district (design doc §10.1). Keep the figure value-separated from the ground so the silhouette still reads.
generation_background.matting_note: This does NOT change the matting pipeline. Alpha is still recovered from white+black plates at the END of the process (sprite-spec.md). Colourful grounds are for identity/turnaround/hero generation, where the goal is the best possible character — not for the final matte plates.
generation_background.supersedes: The flat-green sheet instruction in SKILL.md workflow step 2.1 and prompt-grammar.md turnaround template, for the identity stages.

spend_budget_on: who the character is and what they do, in 1-2 sentences, FIRST
why each garment exists and how it is constructed
footwear as its own dedicated sentence
body shape, posture, weight distribution, what their work did to them
both ends of the lighting range, with named lit objects
cut: no-text / watermark / logo / UI / border boilerplate
no-extra-fingers and other generic anatomy warnings
anything the model already does correctly by default
keep: character-specific safety rules: minors' full coverage, Ryuki's skin dignity, Splash's non-anatomical torso
canon rules a viewer could misread: Kitsune's ears/tails/paws are costume and equipment
a short 'no lettering' clause ONLY where the design contains decals, badges, patches, signage or screens
prompt_policy.evidence: Boilerplate removal caused no defects across three generations. The single text artifact ('SERVICE' on Ren's shirt) traced to the phrase 'service decals' in the prompt, not to the missing exclusion — prefer renaming the element ('small red-orange paint marks') over restoring the boilerplate.
